daily_reality.typical_workday: CNSs spend approximately 26.6% of day providing direct patient care, 22.1% consulting with nurses/staff, 26.5% teaching nurses/staff, and 19.7% leading evidence-based practice projects. No two days are the same — work alternates between office-based planning, research, and writing to being on the unit helping nurses, running codes, running simulations, teaching classes, and running meetings. Work in hospitals, physicians' offices, outpatient clinics, and home healthcare.
daily_reality.seasonality: Less seasonal than bedside nursing. Quality improvement projects may align with fiscal year cycles. Accreditation surveys create peak preparation periods. New graduate orientations increase workload in spring/summer hiring cycles.

laws: State-specific CNS scope of practice laws
State prescriptive authority laws (expanding — Maryland 2025 allows CNS prescribing)
regulatory.licensing: Requires MSN or DNP with CNS specialization. National certification through ANCC or specialty-specific boards. 28 states + DC have full practice authority for APRNs. Maryland (2025) now allows CNS prescribing authority. Wisconsin considering full practice authority legislation. Practice authority varies significantly by state — some require physician collaboration.
regulatory.penalties: License revocation/suspension for practice outside scope. State Board of Nursing disciplinary actions. Malpractice liability. Penalties vary by state — governed by individual Nurse Practice Acts. Wisconsin bill aims to remove physician supervision barriers.
regulatory_bodies: NCSBN (National Council of State Boards of Nursing)

abbreviations: NDNQI - National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators
HCAHPS - Hospital Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers

fears: Role ambiguity and being undervalued in organization
Lack of clear career advancement pathways
Being seen as overhead rather than essential
Scope of practice restrictions limiting effectiveness
Inability to demonstrate ROI of CNS role to administrators
motivation: Improving patient outcomes through evidence-based practice
Mentoring and developing the next generation of nurses
Leading transformational change in healthcare organizations
Intellectual stimulation from research and innovation
Bridging gap between research and clinical practice
Autonomy in shaping nursing practice at organizational level
career_psychology.burnout: CNS burnout driven by role ambiguity, high workload from combining clinical, educational, and leadership responsibilities, and lack of organizational support. Career calling serves as protective factor. Institutions offering leadership tracks and clinical ladder programs see improved morale. CNSs may experience burnout when stuck in routine tasks without advancement opportunities. Recovery experiences and fostering sense of professional calling identified as key mitigation strategies.
